name: VIP (Vasoactive intestinal peptide)

lead: VIP is a natural 28-amino-acid peptide that widens blood vessels, relaxes smooth muscle and modulates immune activity. Users interested in recovery speculate it could improve circulation and help them train and heal better.

It binds VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP in target cells, and its half-life in blood is about two minutes. Human trials of VIP are small and aimed at physiology, headache or lung disease; none tests it for appearance or recovery.

paras: VIP is sold by some vendors as a research peptide and discussed in peptide communities alongside other recovery compounds. There is no established routine, and its short half-life is part of the discussion around how it is used.
Intravenous VIP was used in migraine studies to provoke headache, showing it has vascular effects. No safety data exist for the research-peptide use pattern, and it is not an approved product.

angle.text: VIP is a natural vasodilating neuropeptide sold as a research peptide. Users speculate that widening blood vessels and modulating immune activity could speed recovery, supporting better training and healing. Its established research concerns gut, lung and immune function.

lead: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) is a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide found in the gut, brain, heart, lungs and other tissues. It acts through the VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors and has vasodilating, smooth-muscle-relaxing and immune-modulating effects.[1][2]

VIP is sold online in some peptide markets as a research compound. Published human research on injected VIP itself is limited to small physiological and headache-provocation studies, a Phase 1 study in respiratory distress, and trials of its synthetic form aviptadil.[3][4][5] No study of VIP for appearance was found.

paras: VIP relaxes smooth muscle in the gut, gallbladder and airways, stimulates water and electrolyte secretion in the intestine, and causes coronary and peripheral vasodilation. In the brain, it is an important synchroniser of circadian rhythm in the suprachiasmatic nucleus.[1] A review of its cardiovascular effects notes that it is 50 to 100 times more potent than acetylcholine as a vasodilator on a molar basis.[2]

Clinically, VIP is overproduced in VIPomas, and VIP signalling is altered in inflammatory bowel disease.[1] Its short half-life of about two minutes in blood is one reason analogues such as aviptadil exist.[1]

Small trials have given intravenous VIP to study its effects rather than to treat appearance concerns. In migraine research, infusions in migraine patients and healthy volunteers were used to examine headache and cranial blood-flow responses.[3][4] An early Phase 1 study examined VIP in acute respiratory distress syndrome and sepsis,[5] and a registered study examined VIP in COPD with pulmonary hypertension.[6]
The synthetic analogue aviptadil has been tested in COVID-19 respiratory failure; see the Aviptadil article. No studies of VIP in cosmetic, recovery or performance contexts were found.

VIP is listed by some online vendors as a research compound, with claims about immune and inflammatory regulation. These claims come from marketing and community discussion; no human trial supports them for the uses advertised, and no community threads were found suitable for citation here.
